FacilityOps: Waterfront facilities should initiate heavy-weather procedures, secure or remove hazardous cargoes, and verify that adequate moorings and safe access for vessels are available.

VesselOps: All vessels must complete cargo operations, secure gear, and prepare to clear the channel or moor safely; no inbound traffic without specific Coast Guard approval.
OceanVesselOps: All vessels must complete cargo operations, secure gear, and prepare to clear the channel or moor safely; no inbound traffic without specific Coast Guard approval.
FacilityOps: Port and terminal operators must secure cranes, hazardous materials, and loose equipment, discontinue cargo transfers involving bulk petroleum or hazardous cargoes, and prepare facilities for possible shutdown.

VesselOps: Port closed; no vessel movements permitted and all vessels already in port must be securely moored and remain in port until the condition is lifted.
OceanVesselOps: Port closed; no vessel movements permitted and all vessels already in port must be securely moored and remain in port until the condition is lifted.
FacilityOps: All cargo handling and port operations are suspended; facilities must be secured and all loose equipment and hazardous materials properly stowed.

VesselOps: All vessels in the Port of Virginia should review and implement heavy-weather plans, verify moorings, secure equipment, and remain ready for further Coast Guard direction.
OceanVesselOps: All vessels in the Port of Virginia should review and implement heavy-weather plans, verify moorings, secure equipment, and remain ready for further Coast Guard direction.
FacilityOps: Port facilities should begin securing cranes and cargo-handling gear, clear docks of loose items, verify emergency power, and activate hurricane preparedness procedures.

VesselOps: All vessels should review and activate heavy-weather plans, secure loose gear, reinforce mooring arrangements, and maintain a continuous communications watch with the COTP.
OceanVesselOps: All vessels should review and activate heavy-weather plans, secure loose gear, reinforce mooring arrangements, and maintain a continuous communications watch with the COTP.
FacilityOps: Port and facility operators should begin heavy-weather preparations, secure or stow hazardous cargo, inspect and ready emergency equipment, and prepare for the possible suspension of cargo and bunkering operations as conditions escalate.

VesselOps: Port remains open to all traffic; mariners are advised to exercise caution, monitor weather updates, and begin heavy-weather preparations.
OceanVesselOps: Port remains open to all traffic; mariners are advised to exercise caution, monitor weather updates, and begin heavy-weather preparations.
FacilityOps: Port and facility operators should implement heavy-weather procedures, secure cargo-handling gear and waterfront equipment, and initiate storm preparedness measures.

VesselOps: All vessels must review and implement their heavy-weather mooring or sortie plans, ensure extra mooring lines and chafing gear are ready, and maintain close communication with the Coast Guard.
OceanVesselOps: All vessels must review and implement their heavy-weather mooring or sortie plans, ensure extra mooring lines and chafing gear are ready, and maintain close communication with the Coast Guard.
FacilityOps: Ports and waterfront facilities remain open but must begin securing cargo-handling equipment, remove potential debris and hazardous materials, verify emergency power systems, and review heavy-weather response plans.

VesselOps: All vessels must remove or secure hazardous materials and loose gear, take all practicable measures to maximize stability, maintain a navigation watch and monitor VHF-16, arrange sufficient tug assistance for arrivals and departures, and ensure small craft are hauled out or moored in sheltered locations. Unmanned or “dead” vessels may not remain in the port without notification to the COTP.
OceanVesselOps: All vessels must remove or secure hazardous materials and loose gear, take all practicable measures to maximize stability, maintain a navigation watch and monitor VHF-16, arrange sufficient tug assistance for arrivals and departures, and ensure small craft are hauled out or moored in sheltered locations. Unmanned or “dead” vessels may not remain in the port without notification to the COTP.
FacilityOps: Waterfront facilities must clear docks of potential missile hazards, flying debris, hazardous materials and oil-pollution threats; implement container-stacking limits (maximum two high for hazmat containers, four high for others) or alternate securing arrangements approved by the COTP; secure docks, wharves and piers; notify the COTP of any dangerous cargo that must remain outside; conduct safety surveys and correct hazards within 48 hours; prepare for possible bridge closures, traffic restrictions, and implementation of hurricane pollution contingency and security plans.

VesselOps: All vessels should review and activate heavy-weather plans, secure loose gear, reinforce mooring arrangements, and maintain a continuous communications watch with the COTP.
FacilityOps: Port and facility operators should begin heavy-weather preparations, secure or stow hazardous cargo, inspect and ready emergency equipment, and prepare for the possible suspension of cargo and bunkering operations as conditions escalate.

VesselOps: Mariners are reminded there are no safe havens; under Condition Zulu no vessels may enter or transit the port and all vessel movements are prohibited; under Condition Yankee all vessels, barges and pleasure craft should plan to depart the port early to avoid bridge closures.
FacilityOps: Under Condition Zulu all waterfront operations are suspended except final safety preparations approved by the Captain of the Port, and facility preparations should be complete; ports are safest when the inventory of vessels is at a minimum.
